chapters.name: Edinburgh
chapters.history: Edinburgh grew along a ridge of old volcanic rock, with a castle at one end, a royal palace at the other, and the Royal Mile running between them. By the 1700s the crowded Old Town was bursting at the seams, so the city built the orderly Georgian streets of the New Town across the valley and became the “Athens of the North”: home of the Scottish Enlightenment, of David Hume and Adam Smith, and of the Greek-temple monuments that crown Calton Hill. Scotland’s capital for more than five hundred years, it still wears its history on every stone.

chapters.name: London
chapters.history: The Romans founded Londinium on the Thames almost two thousand years ago, and the square mile they walled is still the City of London. The city survived plague and the Great Fire of 1666, after which Christopher Wren rebuilt more than fifty churches and St Paul’s Cathedral, whose dome has watched over London since the early 1700s. Today glass towers crowd around Wren’s spires, Nelson keeps watch over Trafalgar Square, and the old and the new share every street.

chapters.name: Belfast
chapters.history: Belfast takes its name from Béal Feirste, “the mouth of the sandbank ford”, where the little River Farset met the Lagan. It was a modest town until the 1800s, when linen, rope-making and shipbuilding turned it into an industrial powerhouse. By 1900 Harland & Wolff was the largest shipyard in the world, and in 1911 it launched the Titanic. After the hard decades of the Troubles, the old docks have become the Titanic Quarter, and the Albert Memorial Clock still leans gently over the city centre.

chapters.name: Dublin
chapters.history: Vikings founded Dublin in the 840s beside Dubh Linn, the “black pool” where the River Poddle met the Liffey. Christ Church Cathedral rose on their settlement, and St Patrick’s followed nearby. Georgian Dublin came next, with its grand quays and James Gandon’s green-domed Custom House. In 1759 Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on a brewery at St James’s Gate, which is why a pint here tastes like history. In 1922 Dublin became the capital of an independent Ireland.
